zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical reference: the supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida (CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). It was consulted after independent scan reading. The scan governs spelling, allographs, typography and lineation; the revised transcription and English notes are this review's own. Scan source: BnF Gallica / Bibliothèque nationale de France.

lines.note: Guaratçucaxi gives the transitive or causative noise-making verb, with its principal parts. This is the opening body entry, not a running header; its Portuguese definition continues on c1-l001.
Completes the preceding definition: making a clatter or noise. The short row belongs to Guaratçucaxi, whose opening row has been restored to the body zone.
Guaratçuqi describes a clatter occurring, contrasting with the preceding noise-making verb. The qu and uita principal parts are retained, and the Portuguese definition continues below.
Completes the intransitive noise definition as a crash or noise. This is a separate physical continuation even though its wording repeats c1-l001.
The Japanese explanation means a dragon depicted in a picture. The Portuguese calls it a painted lagarto; the circumflexes in Guareô and reô and the upright written-language label S. are preserved.
This homonymous entry instead describes a recumbent dragon, matching the Portuguese 'that is lying down'. Fuſu has long s, and S. is the separate written-language label.
Guariacu is explained by tiles and stones or pebbles. Portuguese pe- continues as pedras on the next physical row; the visible hyphen is retained.
Completes pedras and begins an example about failing to recognize a precious jewel. The Japanese conditional continues on the next row; Vt is printed in the italic explanatory apparatus.
The example treats the unrecognized jewel as rubble. Xix. is an upright source label, not part of the Japanese sentence; the damaged Portuguese word reads conhecen-, continued as conhecendo below.

runs.text: do as pedras precioſas estimalas como telhas,

lines.note: Completes conhecendo: not recognizing precious stones, one values them as tiles. The sentence supplies the literal explanation of the Japanese example rather than a new entry.

runs.text: ou pedras. i, Quem não conhece as couſas não

lines.note: After 'or stones', i introduces the broader lesson: someone who does not know things does not appreciate them. Its final verb is on the next row.
Completes the proverbial interpretation: such a person does not esteem them. The short line closes Guariacu.
Guaſſui is menstruation, paraphrased by Tçuqino ſauari. The Portuguese word molheres is physically divided after mo without a secure printed hyphen; none is supplied.

Completes molheres and introduces the menstrual flow stopping. Enlargement shows a short second s, while the first s is abraded to a tall stem: Guaſsuiga is selected, with the headword Guaſſui supporting its identity but not overriding that local allograph. The damaged tomaru is compatible with the visible letters and cessation gloss; these worn strokes remain a nonblocking caveat.

runs.text: a molher de fazer ſua regra ordinaria.

lines.note: Completes Deixar: a woman ceases to have her usual menstrual period. This supports the interpretation of tomaru without adding a medical cause not stated in the entry.
Guato is a picture or drawing, with Yezzu as its Japanese equivalent. Fito starts an example about reproducing a person's form.

Continues the example: transfer the appearance of a person or similar subject into a picture. The entire Portuguese Treſ- belongs to the italic translation; the isolated roman T in the draft was not a Japanese fragment.

runs.text: ladar, ou pintar a figura do homem, ou de ou-

lines.note: Completes Tresladar and explains copying or painting a person's figure. The final ou- begins outra on the following physical row.
Completes outra couſa, extending the drawing example to another kind of subject. This closes the picture entry.

Guatô, alternatively doccacu, denotes a particular earthenware lamp container. The scan supports t, a circumflex, and the doubled c in doccacu; the Portuguese reads certo vaſo, not the draft's cento paſo.

runs.text: ro em que tẽ cãdea aceſa ſem parecer de fora.

lines.note: Completes barro and describes a burning lamp held inside the vessel without being visible from outside. The printed abbreviation tẽ and the nasal mark in cãdea remain unexpanded.

runs.text: Lũa q̃ os gentios tẽ como Fotoque.

lines.note: Guattenji is described as the moon treated by non-Christians as a Fotoque. The Portuguese wording is the dictionary's religious description. Fotoque is an embedded Japanese term; its exact font boundary is less distinct than its reading, so the existing italic span is retained and the whole term is flagged for human typeface review.
Guaxacu is another tile-and-stone expression, directly paraphrased by Cauara ixi. The initial G is visible and corrects the draft's C.
Guaxeqi has the same tile-and-stone meaning as Guaxacu. Idem refers back to the immediately preceding entry.

runs.text: Hũa certa taboa com hũa pintura de

lines.note: Guaxǒ denotes a board bearing a picture. The caron distinguishes the printed headword, while the Portuguese description continues with the picture's material and placement.

runs.text: papel pegada que està dependurada nas Teras.

lines.note: The paper picture is pasted to the board, which hangs in temples. Teras is the Japanese temple term used within the Portuguese explanation.
Guaxxocu means a lunar eclipse. Coyoiua starts 'tonight', and guax continues on the next row as the same eclipse word; there is no secure hyphen at this line end.

runs.text: Eſta noite hà eclypſe da lũa.

lines.note: Completes the example: there is a lunar eclipse tonight. The translation reads eclypſe, matching the preceding definition rather than the draft's eolypſe.

GI, alternatively chi, is earth or land, paraphrased by Tçuchi. The large G belongs to this entry and spans two rows; the first following letter is capital I, not the draft's lowercase l. Giuo starts the first example.
Giuo vtçu is glossed as measuring land. The next example begins Giuo na- and continues with raſu; the enlarged G of the preceding row remains visible beside this indented continuation.
Completes narasu, levelling the ground. Giuo fiqu introduces a further earthmoving example whose Portuguese explanation follows below.

runs.text: Cauar a terra de lugar mais alto pera entu-

lines.note: The earthmoving operation excavates soil from a higher place in order to fill another place. Enlargement shows the larger initial C of Cauar; the physical entu- division is retained.

runs.text: lhar algũa coua, ou outro lagar mais baixo.

lines.note: Completes entulhar: filling a hollow or another lower place. The scan prints lagar, with a closed a after l, although lugar would fit the sense; the apparent printed anomaly is preserved rather than silently emended. The tilde remains over u in algũa.

runs.text: Almorreimas, ou doença de vazar ſan-

lines.note: This Gi denotes haemorrhoids or a disorder involving bleeding. The initial is G, not B, and ſan- continues as sangue below; the historical disease name is not modernized.
Completes sangue and gives the Japanese example for suffering from this condition. The historical vazzurǒ form and its caron are retained; dal- is part of the following Portuguese disease expression.

runs.text: morreimas, ou de verter ſangue por baixo.

lines.note: Completes the disease expression and explains bleeding from below. Baixo is one word in the scan, not the draft's artificial ba ixo division.

runs.text: O deſquitarſe não ganhando nem perdendo

lines.note: This separate Gi concerns breaking even rather than the medical sense above. Its definition explicitly contrasts neither winning nor losing.
Completes 'in play' and lists alternative Japanese ways of declaring a draw or even result. The lowercase l markers introduce alternatives and are not Japanese syllables.
Adds forms for arriving at an even result, followed by the repeated Portuguese definition. The Japanese maitta is retained as printed rather than expanded into a modern explanatory phrase.
Completes the definition of breaking even: neither winning nor losing. This closes the gaming sense of Gi.
Giacuſuru describes being excessively attached to something. The final de is the first part of the following demasiadamente, not an independently interpreted preposition in this lineated text.
Completes demasiadamente and specifies attachment to some thing. The line continues the degree of attachment rather than starting a new gloss.

runs.text: Certo ponto, ou ſentença que dão os

lines.note: Giacugo is a point or saying supplied in connection with meditation. The people who supply it and the relation to the preceding meditation are specified below.

runs.text: Ienxũs a cerca da meditação precedente.

lines.note: Completes the definition with the Zen-group designation Ienxũs and a reference to the preceding meditation. The embedded denomination and its nasal abbreviation remain as printed.

Giacuxin denotes an attached heart or strong affection. The scan supports the ending xin, not the draft's xun, and the Portuguese Coração afeiçoado corrects the damaged OCR without modernizing the wording.
The first de completes grãde across the line break; the second de introduces the object of affection. Both occurrences are therefore retained rather than collapsed as a supposed duplication.
Giacuxiqi is a painting in several colours. The entire short Portuguese definition belongs to this headword.
Giacuye is explained by putting on clothing. The Portuguese begins with donning a habit or garment and continues on the following indented row.
Completes the clothing definition and gives Giacuye qippan, dressing and eating. The example begins with G, not the draft's C; Ves- visibly uses short s at this line end.
Completes Vestir and supplies comer, matching the paired activities in Giacuye qippan. This continuation is indented in the scan, not aligned as a new entry.
Giaraxi denotes a landward or land-origin wind, described as vento terrenho. The form belongs to the earth/land vocabulary and need not be parsed from the draft kana syllable grouping alone.
Giban is a foundation or preparation. Vt introduces the following example about laying that foundation.
Gibanuo ſuyuru means setting or laying the foundation. The initial G is visible in the example and replaces the draft's C.
The gloss also covers making preparations. A new example begins Gibanno ſu-, with its verb continued below; the visible hyphen is retained.
Completes suuatta fito: a person whose foundation is settled, hence someone determined and steadfast. The Portuguese abbreviations Homẽ and conſtãte remain unexpanded.
Gibat concerns subduing enemies, as the Japanese paraphrase and Portuguese destruction gloss agree. The Portuguese enemy word begins ini-, not the draft's tni-.

runs.text: migos, ou pacificar o reyno principalmente

lines.note: Completes inimigos and adds pacifying the kingdom. Principalmente leads into the usage qualification on the next physical row.
The expression is said chiefly of a king. This qualification closes the royal-pacification entry.
Gibiǒ denotes a person's habitual or constitutionally recurring illness. The scan supports the complete headword and its caron; the draft's zabix was not a usable Japanese reading.
The examples are stone disease and migraine. They explain the habitual-illness sense without specifying a single disease as the headword's meaning.

runs.text: Capela, ou oratorio, onde ſe poem

lines.note: Gibutdǒ is a chapel or private oratory. The Portuguese sentence continues with the devotional image placed there; the Japanese checked t and final caron are retained.

runs.text: o idolo, ou imagem aque cada hũ tem deuação.

lines.note: The oratory houses the idol or image to which a person is devoted. Idolo corrects the draft's adolo, while the printed aque and deuação are not silently modernized.
Gicai means keeping precepts, paraphrased by Caimonuo tamotçu. The Portuguese object of guardar follows on the next row.
Completes 'laws or commandments' and begins a description of an observant person. The Japanese reads giritno, with r and a checked t, rather than the draft's ginitno.
Fito nari completes the statement that the person observes the precepts. The Portuguese adjective obseruante is divided after obſer-.
Completes observance of the laws. The upright S. is the written-language usage label, separate from the italic Portuguese sentence.
Gichǔ means within the earth, directly matched by Tçuchino naca and the Portuguese gloss. The mark over u is a caron in this occurrence.
Gicqin concerns close or intimate attendance on a lord. The cq cluster and the long-u mark in Mutçumaxǔ are retained; Qimino begins the explanatory phrase continued below.
The Japanese is a person at the lord's side. Portuguese priuado identifies a confidant or close attendant, not simply someone physically nearby.
Completes the description of an attendant who is always in the lord's presence. The relative clause belongs with the preceding priuado definition.
Gidadauo fumu introduces stamping the feet. The headword's dada is retained as printed rather than normalized to a more familiar modern form.

runs.text: ou bater com os pees no chão com hũa maneira

lines.note: The action is striking the ground with the feet in a certain manner. Maneira corrects the draft's mancira; the rhythmic description continues below.
The stamping has a hurried rhythm. Gidagidato suru is given as another expression, with the final verb divided at the physical line break.
Ru completes suru, and Idem gives it the same stamping meaning. This short continuation must remain separate from Gidai below.
Gidai denotes the earth element. The short definition treats earth as an element rather than a parcel of land.

Gidameqi describes making a clattering noise. The abbreviated principal part u is printed as such; it is not silently expanded to qu even though the verb's linguistic identification suggests that fuller form.

runs.text: quando hum bate com os pees no chão.

lines.note: Stamping the feet on the ground exemplifies the noise. The line completes the comparison introduced by como.
Gigimecaxi concerns causing a crash or clatter. The displayed u principal part is retained literally, with the fuller caſu form appearing in the example below.

runs.text: traquinada com as armas, ou puxãdo por alguẽ

lines.note: The noise may be made with weapons or by pulling someone. The abbreviated endings puxãdo and alguẽ are preserved; the person's resistance is specified on the next row.
Completes the case of a person unwilling to come. A new example concerns making a horse clatter or stamp, beginning Vmauo gigime-.

runs.text: Fazer traquinada com o caualo deten-

lines.note: Completes gigimecaſu and starts the explanation of holding a horse in place while making it stamp. The Portuguese deten- continues below.

runs.text: doo em hum lugar, & fazendoo bater com os

lines.note: Completes detendoo and adds making the horse strike with its feet. The scan shows fazendoo, including the object-pronoun o lost in the draft's fazendo.
Completes the horse's stamping action. The printed pees has two e letters, not the draft's pes.
Gigimeqi is the corresponding occurrence of a noisy clatter. The Portuguese eſtrondo includes t, and eſ- begins estas on the next row; the printed principal part u is retained.

runs.text: tas couſas, ou fazerſe traquinada com os

lines.note: Completes estas couſas, referring back to the noisy objects and actions above. The alternative description of clattering with the feet continues below.
Completes the foot-noise description. Again the scan prints pees with two e letters.
Gigiǒ is a thing that is certain or determined. The caron and the draft's close Couſacerta word separation are retained rather than regularized from modern Portuguese expectations.
Gigue and the two alternative forms designate local people or residents. The Portuguese na- continues as naturais below; the punctuation following the first l is retained.

runs.text: turais, ou moradores do Machi, ou pouoação

lines.note: Completes naturais and describes residents of a Machi or settlement. Machi is a Japanese town term embedded in the Portuguese explanation; no terminal punctuation is supplied where none is secure.
The alternative headwords refer the reader back to Gigue. Both initial G letters correct OCR C; the upright Gigue after the Portuguese Vide is a cross-reference term within the explanatory apparatus.
Giguiǒ is the configuration or situation of the ground, paraphrased by Gino catachi. The initial in Gino is G, and Portuguese ſitio has i rather than the draft's second t.
Completes dalgum and specifies a place or piece of ground. The line belongs to the topographical description above.
Gigocu is hell. The example begins falling into hell; its initial G and the printed tç cluster are retained.
Ru completes votçuru, falling into hell. Inferno corrects the draft's interno; the separate Gijin. at the far right is a catchword and is encoded as furniture, not repeated in this body line.
